title: the claim behind the bread
hook: a white dress, a party, a wafer: and the claim the day was about
tomorrow: the most misunderstood room in the building

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sign of the cross, all of you in two seconds. Today, the thing at the center of every Mass.

A white dress or a clip-on tie. Photos on the church steps, a cake after. First Communion is easy to remember. What the day was actually about can be fuzzier: in surveys, a lot of Catholics describe the bread as a symbol. The Church's own claim is much bigger than a symbol. So here it is, once, plainly.
screen: `A WHITE DRESS. A CAKE.` → `A SYMBOL?` → `THE CLAIM, ONCE, PLAINLY.`

segments.voice: It starts the night before Jesus died, at a Passover meal. He takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it and says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me." Gave thanks, in Greek, is where the word comes from: eucharistia, thanksgiving. Now the claim. Catholics believe that when the priest says those words at Mass, the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ. They still look, taste and feel like bread and wine. What they are, underneath, has changed. Not a symbol of him: him. The Church calls it the real presence. In John's Gospel, Jesus calls himself the living bread, and many followers find that too hard and walk away. He lets them go. After Mass, the consecrated bread that's left is kept in a small box near the altar, the tabernacle, with a red lamp burning beside it. That's why people bend a knee when they walk into an empty church. They believe he's there. Christians differ here. Orthodox Christians and Lutherans also speak of a real presence; many other Protestants see the meal as a memorial and a sign.
screen: `THIS IS MY BODY.` · `EUCHARISTIA — THANKSGIVING.` · `STILL LOOKS LIKE BREAD.` · `THE TABERNACLE AND THE LAMP.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Think of a time someone simply stayed with you: in a waiting room, on the end of your bed, on the phone. They didn't fix anything. Breathe in, remembering it. Breathe out slowly.
The Eucharist. Thanksgiving: the bread and wine Catholics believe become Christ himself, his real presence. Second word.
screen: `THE EUCHARIST — your 2nd word` → clicks onto the strand beside the sign of the cross.

segments.voice: Your line: he stayed. It's what the red lamp is saying, in an empty church on a Tuesday afternoon. Day two, done.

screen: `DAY 2 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MOST MISUNDERSTOOD ROOM IN THE BUILDING.`

howItsDone: Catholics receive the Eucharist at Mass, genuflect toward the tabernacle when entering a church, and many spend quiet time in prayer before it, a practice called adoration.

story.title: the day the crowd walked away
story.text: A crowd that ate bread by the lakeside the day before follows Jesus, hoping for more. He tells them he is the living bread, and that his flesh is real food. It's too much. Many who had been following him turn around and go home. He doesn't call after them or soften it. He turns to his twelve closest friends and asks if they're leaving too, and Peter answers: Lord, to whom would we go?

wrong.myth: the Church teaches communion is a symbol.
wrong.truth: its teaching is the real presence: the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood, while still looking like bread and wine.
